p: It is very late. The fire has burned down, Tacitus is snoring, and Mrs Pruett has twice put her head round the door to ask whether I mean to sit up all night again. I do not, but I wish to set down a few last thoughts while the long road we have travelled together is fresh in my mind.

We began in the darkness of Africa, millions of years ago, with a creature that stood up on two legs and picked up a stone. We have ended with machines that talk. Between the two lies everything: the hearth and the grave, the plough and the city, the alphabet and the coin, the law of Hammurabi and the Great Charter, the sages of the Axial Age, the empires that rose and fell, the plagues, the presses, the ships, the engines, the wars, and the slow, unfinished, often reversed but never wholly abandoned extension of dignity to more and more of the human race.

Is there a pattern in it? Mr Gibbon thought history little more than the register of the crimes, follies and misfortunes of mankind. Many of my contemporaries think it a story of continual progress, with the British Empire as its happy ending. The pages from the future have cured me of the second opinion, and my own studies have always kept me from the first. If I must say what I have learned, it is this.

First, that the greatest changes are rarely the ones that the people living through them notice. No one knew that the Neolithic Revolution was happening. The coffee house seemed a fashion, the telegraph a convenience, the first calculating engines a toy. The things that change the world tend to arrive quietly, in the workshop and the kitchen, while everyone is watching the battle.

Second, that every gift has its price, and that the price is often paid by someone other than the receiver. Farming fed the many and enslaved some of them. Sugar sweetened the tea of England and was grown by the enslaved of Jamaica. The steam engine clothed the world and blackened its air. I do not say this to condemn our ancestors, but to remind us to ask, of every new marvel, who is paying for it.

Third, that civilisation is more fragile than it looks, and more resilient. Rome fell; the Bronze Age kingdoms fell; the Indus cities were forgotten. Yet the knowledge was carried on, in Constantinople and Baghdad, in monasteries and in memory, and the human story resumed. The men of the future face dangers far greater than any I have described: weapons that could end all life, a climate their own engines have disturbed, machines whose nature they do not yet understand. I cannot tell them how their story ends. I can tell them that their ancestors survived the Ice Age, the Black Death and the twentieth century, and that they are descended exclusively from survivors.

And last, that the great engine of history is not the conqueror, nor the machine, but the ordinary capacity of human beings to talk to one another: to argue, to teach, to remember, to persuade and to change their minds. It began around a fire. It continues, I am told, around a small slab of glass. I hope it never stops.
Thank you for listening to an old man for so long. If you have heard every word, you have shown more patience than any of my pupils at Oxford, and very nearly as much as Tacitus. Good night.
